title: SWE-bench
markdown:
SWE-bench is an evaluation framework for language models using software engineering problems drawn from real GitHub issues and corresponding pull requests [1](#source-1).

The SWE-bench benchmark described in the paper contains 2,294 software engineering problems [1](#source-1).

The SWE-bench benchmark described in the paper draws its problems from 12 popular Python repositories [1](#source-1).

Each SWE-bench task provides a codebase and a description of an issue to be resolved [1](#source-1).

According to the paper authors, resolving SWE-bench issues in the supplied codebase requires editing the existing codebase to address the described issue [1](#source-1).

According to the paper authors, resolving SWE-bench issues frequently requires understanding and coordinating simultaneous changes across functions, classes, and files [1](#source-1).

## Origins and publication

The SWE-bench paper describes the SWE-bench evaluation framework [1](#source-1).

Carlos E. Jimenez coauthored the SWE-bench paper [1](#source-1).

John Yang coauthored the SWE-bench paper [1](#source-1).

Alexander Wettig coauthored the SWE-bench paper [1](#source-1).

Shunyu Yao coauthored the SWE-bench paper [1](#source-1).

Kexin Pei coauthored the SWE-bench paper [1](#source-1).

Ofir Press coauthored the SWE-bench paper [1](#source-1).

Karthik Narasimhan coauthored the SWE-bench paper [1](#source-1).

The SWE-bench paper's first arXiv version was submitted on October 10, 2023 [1](#source-1).

The SWE-bench paper's third arXiv version was submitted on November 11, 2024 [1](#source-1).

The project documentation reports the SWE-bench paper as accepted for an oral presentation at ICLR 2024 [2](#source-2).

The authors frame SWE-bench as using real-world software engineering as a rich, sustainable, and challenging testbed for evaluating the next generation of language models [1](#source-1).

The SWE-bench authors describe effective language-model evaluation as outpaced by language models [1](#source-1).

The SWE-bench authors describe studying frontier language-model capabilities as essential for future language-model development [1](#source-1).

The SWE-bench paper describes advances on SWE-bench as steps toward more practical, intelligent, and autonomous language models [1](#source-1).

## Method and implementation

A SWE-bench task supplies a codebase and a description of an issue to be resolved [1](#source-1).

The project documentation describes SWE-bench’s expected model output, given a codebase and an issue, as a patch resolving that issue [2](#source-2).

According to its authors, SWE-bench uses real GitHub issues and corresponding pull requests as its problem sources across Python repositories [1](#source-1).

SWE-bench tasks require editing the supplied codebase to address the issue [1](#source-1).

## Evaluation and limitations

The project documentation describes the Docker-based SWE-bench evaluation harness as intended for reproducible evaluation with consistent results [2](#source-2).

The project documentation reports the evaluation harness as fully containerized using Docker [2](#source-2).

The documentation reports SWE-bench cloud-based evaluations via Modal [2](#source-2).

SWE-bench documentation lists its installation guide as a guide for local and cloud setup [2](#source-2).

SWE-bench documentation lists its evaluation guide as a guide to evaluating models on SWE-bench [2](#source-2).

SWE-bench documentation lists its harness API documentation as a reference for the evaluation harness [2](#source-2).

SWE-bench documentation lists its inference API documentation as a reference for model inference [2](#source-2).

The documentation reports a full SWE-bench leaderboard on the project website [2](#source-2).

The authors report evaluating their fine-tuned model SWE-Llama on SWE-bench [1](#source-1).

Claude 2 was evaluated on SWE-bench in the experiments reported by the authors [1](#source-1).

The paper qualitatively describes SWE-Llama as resolving only the simplest issues in its original SWE-bench evaluations [1](#source-1).

The paper qualitatively describes the evaluated state-of-the-art proprietary models as resolving only the simplest issues in its original SWE-bench evaluations [1](#source-1).

review.originalMarkdown:
SWE-bench is a benchmark for evaluating language models on real-world software engineering problems drawn from GitHub issues and their corresponding pull requests [1](#source-1). The original benchmark comprises 2,294 problems from 12 popular Python repositories, with each task asking a model to edit a codebase to address a described issue [1](#source-1). Its focus is on modifying existing software, including tasks that require coordinated changes across multiple functions, classes, or files, rather than traditional code generation alone [1](#source-1).

## Origins and research purpose

SWE-bench was introduced in the paper *SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?* by Carlos E. Jimenez, John Yang, Alexander Wettig, Shunyu Yao, Kexin Pei, Ofir Press, and Karthik Narasimhan [1](#source-1). The paper was first submitted to arXiv as a preprint on October 10, 2023, and its third version was posted on November 11, 2024 [1](#source-1). The project documentation records its acceptance for an oral presentation at the 2024 International Conference on Learning Representations [2](#source-2).

The authors presented real-world software engineering as a rich, sustainable, and challenging setting for evaluating language-model capabilities [1](#source-1). Their motivation was that improvements in language models had outpaced the ability to evaluate them effectively, making more demanding assessments necessary [1](#source-1). The benchmark was intended to investigate capabilities associated with more practical and autonomous language models through the concrete task of resolving software issues [1](#source-1).

## Task design

A SWE-bench task supplies a codebase and a description of an issue that needs to be resolved [1](#source-1). The expected model output is a patch that addresses the described problem in that codebase [2](#source-2). The problems originate in actual GitHub issues and associated pull requests across the benchmark’s Python repositories [1](#source-1).

According to the introductory paper, resolving these issues frequently requires understanding and coordinating modifications across several parts of a software project [1](#source-1). The authors identify interaction with execution environments, processing extremely long contexts, and complex reasoning as demands of the benchmark [1](#source-1). They contrast these requirements with those of traditional code generation tasks, emphasizing the difficulty of making changes within existing software [1](#source-1).

## Evaluation and initial results

The project provides a Docker-based evaluation harness intended to make evaluations reproducible and results consistent [2](#source-2). Its documentation dates the release of the fully containerized harness to June 27, 2024, and records the addition of cloud-based evaluation through Modal on January 11, 2025 [2](#source-2). The same documentation provides access to the dataset through Hugging Face, installation instructions, evaluation guides, and references for the harness and inference interfaces [2](#source-2). A project leaderboard is available through the SWE-bench website [2](#source-2).

In the evaluations reported in the introductory paper, the authors tested proprietary language models as well as their fine-tuned model, SWE-Llama [1](#source-1). Claude 2 was the best-performing model in those reported experiments, resolving 1.96% of the issues [1](#source-1). The authors characterized the evaluated models as capable of resolving only the simplest issues in the benchmark [1](#source-1).

## Related datasets and variants

The project documentation distinguishes the original SWE-bench dataset from SWE-bench Lite, SWE-bench Verified, and SWE-bench Multimodal [2](#source-2). SWE-bench Verified was released on August 13, 2024, with 500 problems described by the project as engineer-confirmed solvable [2](#source-2). The documentation also records integration of SWE-bench Multimodal with private test-split evaluation on January 13, 2025 [2](#source-2).

Alongside these datasets, the project lists SWE-Llama 7b and 13b models, including versions labeled “PEFT” [2](#source-2). It also provides retrieval resources labeled “Oracle” and BM25, together with documentation for creating retrieval-augmented generation datasets [2](#source-2).
